segments.text: Most people think working with AI means sitting at a keyboard trying to type one single flawless prompt to get a perfect answer on the first try.
Think back to the best group project you ever did in history class.
You sat around a table, brainstormed and shared ideas.
You figured out what parts of the project were missing and you worked together to improve the draft step by step.
That is exactly how you should approach AI.
It is a two-person group project, consisting of just you and the machine.
Getting the best possible result takes a back-and-forth conversation, not a single command.
The first move is to use AI as a thought partner.
You bounce ideas off each other to see what sticks, but you always make the final decisions.
Looking at this interface, the student starts the conversation.
I'd like to earn money this summer by starting a small business.
Can we talk through what might fit me?
The AI replies with a question about your skills rather than an immediate answer.
What are you already good at and what problems do people around you regularly need help solving?
The student answers, I'm good with dogs and teaching younger kids math.
The AI synthesizes that input into a plan.
That gives us three realistic directions, pet care, math tutoring and a neighborhood errand service,
which sounds most interesting to you and which would be easiest to start.
A good conversation asks about you before it answers.
The second move is using AI as a learning tool when a concept doesn't quite make sense.
You ask it to explain, follow up on the confusing parts, connect the idea to something you already know,
and then explain it back in your own words to check if you missed anything.
In this example, the student asks, I might start a business this summer mowing lawns.
What is profit and how do I calculate it?
Explain it using simple numbers that apply to a lawn mowing business.
The AI answers, profit is the money left after you subtract every cost from your sales.
It then provides a specific example.
For example, your sales are $300.
Your total costs are $150, leaving you with $150 in profit.
The formula is sales minus costs equals profit.
Ask AI to explain the idea using a situation you know.
Sometimes you face a massive decision and have absolutely no idea where to start.
The third move is asking AI to help you find that starting point.
Looking at this board, the student sets strict rules.
I need to start thinking about college, but I don't know where to begin.
Ask me one question at a time to help me figure out what matters to me.
Don't recommend a college yet.
Respecting those constraints, the AI offers a single foundational question.
Do you already have a career or field in mind?
Or do you want college to help you explore different possibilities?
When you don't know where to begin, ask AI for the first question.
The fourth move is working with AI over several rounds to improve your work.
That process is called iteration.
To iterate means to build something in versions, using each version to improve the next.
Here we see an early round of conversation where the student gives a vague prompt.
Give me ideas for a summer business.
The AI returns a generic list.
Here are some ideas, lawn care, pet sitting, tutoring, car washing, and selling crafts online.
Contrast that with a later round.
The student provides specific details.
I'm considering a lawn cutting business.
I'll serve homes within biking distance, use the customer's mower, work week-day afternoons,
and charge by lawn size.
Help me find weaknesses in the plan and improve it.
Now the AI acts as a pressure tester.
Let's pressure test it.
How will you quote lawn sizes?
What happens when it rains?
Better details give AI better material to improve.
The next level starts after the first answer.
Explore ideas, build understanding, and improve together.
